top_result_summaries.title: Notes from the Field: Initial Public Health Response to a Measles Outbreak in a Close-Knit West Texas Community — January−February 2025  | MMWR
top_result_summaries.snippet: A measles outbreak occurred in Texas during January–August 2025. During January 29–February 28, 2025, Texas reported 207 confirmed measles cases, primarily among members of a close-knit west Texas community. Measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine and measles testing clinics were offered; however, community members were hesitant to interact with public health and health care systems, and MMR vaccine acceptance was low. In challenging community contexts, public health messaging intended to limit viral transmission and severe health outcomes could supplement standard control measures, including advising persons with suspected measles to avoid contact with other persons to prevent transmission and to seek medical care promptly. On January 29, 2025, the South Plains Public Health District (SPPHD) alerted the Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) Public Health Region 1 of an unvaccinated school-aged child with measles in Gaines County, a rural county in west Texas bordering New Mexico.

top_result_summaries.title: Confirmed Case of Measles - January 2025 | Texas DSHS
top_result_summaries.snippet: The Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) is reporting two confirmed cases of measles in residents of Harris County. We advise clinicians to follow the recommendations below and report any suspected cases to your local health department immediately, preferably while the patient is in your presence. HHD has published a list of possible exposure locations and dates where members of the public may have been exposed to measles during the patients’ infectious periods. Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommend children receive one dose of MMR at 12 to 15 months of age and another at 4 to 6 years. * If a measles case is identified in a healthcare setting, including outpatient and long-term care facilities, the following measures should be taken: Interim Infection Prevention and Control Recommendations for Measles in Healthcare Settings | Infection Control | CDC.

top_result_summaries.title: Characteristics of Patients Hospitalized with Measles During an Outbreak — West Texas, January–March 2025  | MMWR
top_result_summaries.snippet: During the first 3 months of a large measles outbreak in the South Plains region of west Texas (January 20–March 18, 2025), 325 measles cases were reported; 60 (18.5%) patients were hospitalized. Among 54 hospitalized patients with available medical records, all were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status, 91% were aged <18 years, approximately 70% had pneumonia and hypoxia, and one patient died. On January 29, 2025, the Texas Department of State Health Services Public Health Region 1 was notified by the South Plains Public Health District of a case of measles in an unvaccinated school-aged child. During January 20–March 18, 2025, a total of 325 confirmed measles cases were reported; 60 (18.5%) patients were hospitalized. During the investigation, 325 confirmed measles cases were reported in the South Plains region of west Texas, with rash or symptom onset dating to January 20, 2025, including 60 (18.5%) patients who were hospitalized.

The Texas outbreak involved the measles genotype D8, and was linked to cases in New Mexico, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Chihuahua, Mexico "Chihuahua (state)").

decision.decision_reason: Iteration 1 produced strong foundational coverage from CDC MMWR, Texas DSHS, and Wikipedia, confirming the outbreak's existence, key localities (Gaines County, West Texas/South Plains, Harris County), and partial case/death/hospitalization figures. However, several critical gaps remain for the Jan–Apr 2025 window: (1) The DSHS main outbreak page (dshs.texas.gov/news-alerts/measles-outbreak-2025) references specific dated press releases (Feb 26 first death, Apr 6 second death) that were not individually surfaced as candidates — these are the primary authoritative sources for death counts within the task window; (2) The DSHS Jan 2025 Harris County alert mentions only 2 cases, while the outbreak page references a much larger cumulative count — intermediate DSHS press releases covering March and April 2025 case milestones are missing; (3) The April 6 second death announcement and April 7 expanded outbreak counties health alert are directly within the task window and not yet captured as discrete source candidates; (4) CDC's national measles case count tracker (separate from MMWR) and any DSHS weekly situation report updates for March–April 2025 have not been surfaced; (5) News coverage from Texas Tribune, local Lubbock/West Texas outlets, and AP/Reuters for the Feb–Apr 2025 period (covering the death announcements and case escalation) is underrepresented — only 1 Texas Tribune result appeared. A second iteration targeting these specific gaps will materially improve coverage of deaths, locality detail, and dated case milestones within the task window.
decision.coverage_assessment: Partial. Core outbreak confirmed with strong MMWR and DSHS anchor sources. Case counts for Jan 20–Mar 18 (325 cases, 60 hospitalizations, 1 death) and Jan 29–Feb 28 (207 confirmed) are evidenced. The DSHS main outbreak page snippet references two deaths within the task window (Feb 26 and Apr 6 announcements) and an April 7 expanded counties alert, but these individual press releases are not yet discrete candidates. Harris County cases (2 confirmed, January 2025) are captured. The April 15 snapshot of 561 cases from Texas Children's is noted. Gaps: (a) DSHS individual press releases for Feb 26 death, Apr 6 second death, Apr 7 health alert; (b) CDC national measles tracker state-level table for Texas; (c) March–April 2025 DSHS situation updates with cumulative counts; (d) Local/regional news for death announcements and county-level detail in the Apr 2025 period.
decision.source_diversity_assessment: Good diversity across federal (CDC/MMWR), state (DSHS, TEPHI), academic (PMC), hospital (Texas Children's), international (WHO, PAHO), and news (Texas Tribune, CIDRAP) tiers. Missing: individual DSHS dated press releases for the two deaths and April health alert; local West Texas news outlets (Lubbock Avalanche-Journal, Plainview Herald); AP/Reuters wire coverage of death announcements; CDC national measles case count table (non-MMWR).
decision.trustworthiness_assessment: High for existing candidates. CDC MMWR reports are peer-reviewed federal surveillance publications — highest trust tier. DSHS official pages are primary subnational authority. Texas Children's Hospital page cites DSHS figures directly. PMC article is peer-reviewed but early (Feb 2025 snapshot, 48 cases) — useful for early-period corroboration. Wikipedia is useful for cross-referencing but not a primary source. TEPHI (Texas Epidemic Public Health Institute) is a state-affiliated academic body — moderate-high trust. CIDRAP and Texas Tribune are reputable secondary sources. No low-credibility or fringe sources identified.
decision.disease_location_time_fit_assessment: Excellent fit. All top results are directly about measles in Texas in 2025, with dates falling within or overlapping the Jan 1–Apr 30 2025 task window. The MMWR hospitalization report covers Jan 20–Mar 18 2025 (within window). The DSHS outbreak page references events through April 2025 (within window). The Harris County alert is January 2025 (within window). The April 15 Texas Children's snapshot is within window. The DSHS Aug 12 final update page is outside the window but references dated sub-events (Feb 26, Apr 6, Apr 7) that fall within it.
decision.corroboration_potential_assessment: Strong corroboration potential exists for the second iteration. The DSHS Feb 26 and Apr 6 death press releases, if surfaced, would directly corroborate the death count (2 within task window) with dated official evidence quotes. The CDC national measles tracker would cross-validate cumulative Texas case counts. Local news coverage of the death announcements would provide additional dated evidence quotes with locality detail (Lubbock mentioned in Wikipedia snippet for two child deaths). These sources are highly likely to exist and be findable via targeted queries.

The Texas Department of State Health Services is reporting the second measles death of a Texas resident in the ongoing outbreak centered in the state's South Plains region. As of April 4, 481 cases of measles have been confirmed in the outbreak since late January. Most of the cases are in children. During a measles outbreak, about one in five children who get sick will need hospital care and one in 20 will develop pneumonia. People who think they have measles or may have been exposed to measles should isolate themselves and call their health care provider before arriving to be tested. It is important to let the provider know that the patient may have measles and to get instructions on how to come to the office for diagnosis without exposing other people to the virus. top_result_summaries.title: Measles Update — United States, January 1–April 17, 2025 | MMWR
top_result_summaries.snippet: Although measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000, large outbreaks with 50 or more cases have become more frequent, especially in close-knit communities with low vaccination coverage. During January 1–April 17, 2025, a total of 800 measles cases were reported in the United States, the second highest annual case count in 25 years; 82% were associated with an ongoing outbreak in close-knit communities with low vaccination coverage in New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Texas. As of April 17, a total of 800 cases have been reported in the United States in 2025; 654 (82%) cases in New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Texas have been associated with the ongoing outbreak. Overall, 771 (96%) patients have been unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status (77% were unvaccinated, and 14% had unknown vaccination status when excluding 590 cases reported by Texas, which requires explicit consent by law [i.e., opt-in] to enroll in the Texas Immunization Registry), 85 (11%) patients have been hospitalized, and three patients have died.

decision.decision_reason: Two full iterations (8 queries, 44 accepted candidates across both rounds) have been executed against the highest-priority source types. The current candidate pool covers all critical target fields for the Jan 1–Apr 30 2025 Texas measles task window with strong authoritative corroboration. Continuing would exceed the max_iterations: 2 bound and is unlikely to yield materially new evidence given the saturation already achieved across DSHS, CDC MMWR, and news channels.
decision.coverage_assessment:
Coverage is strong across all target fields:

• **cases_confirmed**: Multiple authoritative snapshots captured — 207 cases (Jan 29–Feb 28, MMWR mm7523a2), 325 cases (Jan 20–Mar 18, MMWR mm7520a1), 481 cases (as of Apr 4, DSHS second-death press release), 561 cases (as of Apr 15, Texas Children's), 800 US total with Texas as dominant contributor (Jan 1–Apr 17, MMWR mm7414a1). These provide a time-series of confirmed case milestones within the task window.

• **deaths**: Two Texas deaths within the task window are documented — DSHS Feb 26 press release (first death) and DSHS Apr 6 press release (second death, 481 cases as of Apr 4). Both DSHS press release URLs are now captured as discrete candidates (iter2_q1 surfaced the second-death page directly). The MMWR mm7520a1 confirms 1 death in the Jan 20–Mar 18 sub-period.

• **hospitalizations**: 60 hospitalizations (Jan 20–Mar 18, MMWR mm7520a1); 85 US hospitalizations as of Apr 17 (MMWR mm7414a1); 99+ hospitalizations referenced in Wikipedia (full outbreak arc, useful for upper bound). Texas Children's page (Apr 15) provides a hospital-level snapshot.

• **subnational_location / locality**: Gaines County, South Plains region, West Texas, Lubbock, Seminole (Reinlander Mennonite Church), Harris County all documented. SPPHD PDF (iter2) adds granular locality detail (Gaines County Ag Barn, mobile clinic locations).

• **date_reported**: Multiple dated milestones: Jan 29 (first case), Feb 26 (first death), Apr 4 (481 cases), Apr 6 (second death), Apr 7 (expanded counties health alert), Apr 15 (561 cases), Apr 17 (800 US cases).

• **source_url / source_type / evidence_quote**: All major source URLs are captured as candidates from authoritative domains (dshs.texas.gov, cdc.gov). Evidence quotes are available in snippets for all key data points.

• **cases_probable / cases_suspected / cases_unspecified**: Not explicitly broken out in available snippets; DSHS outbreak page (when fetched) may contain this breakdown. The MMWR reports use "confirmed" classification consistently. This minor gap is acceptable — the task window's confirmed case counts are well-documented.

• **Non-West-Texas cases**: Harris County (2 confirmed, Jan 2025) captured from iter1. The DSHS outbreak page references a "Cases Not Associated with the Outbreak in West Texas" section that will be accessible when the main outbreak page is fetched.
decision.source_diversity_assessment:
Source diversity is excellent across 14+ distinct domains over two iterations:
- Official US federal: cdc.gov (MMWR, national tracker)
- Official Texas state: dshs.texas.gov (outbreak page, press releases, SPPHD PDF, news index)
- Official Texas regional: tephi.texas.gov
- Hospital/clinical: texaschildrens.org
- International: who.int, paho.org
- Academic: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, publichealth.jhu.edu
- News wire/national: nbcnews.com, abcnews.com, cidrap.umn.edu
- Local/regional: texastribune.org
- Reference: en.wikipedia.org (useful for context, not primary)

The only underrepresented channel is local West Texas print/broadcast (Lubbock Avalanche-Journal, KCBD) — however, the DSHS press releases and MMWR reports provide sufficient authoritative coverage of the death and case count data that local news would only corroborate, not add new data points. This gap does not warrant a third iteration.
decision.trustworthiness_assessment:
Trust signals are strong:
- All primary case count and death data traces to dshs.texas.gov (official state health authority) and cdc.gov/mmwr (peer-reviewed federal surveillance reports).
- MMWR reports are authored by named CDC/DSHS investigators and carry standard epidemiological methodology disclosures.
- The DSHS second-death press release (Apr 6) is a discrete, dated official announcement — the highest-trust source for the second death within the task window.
- The SPPHD PDF is an official regional health district presentation, providing granular locality and timeline data with institutional authorship.
- News sources (Texas Tribune, NBC News, CIDRAP) consistently cite DSHS or CDC as their data source, making them acceptable corroborating sources for locality and hospitalization detail.
- Wikipedia is present but flagged as non-primary; it is useful only for contextual cross-checking.
- Facebook, YouTube results were surfaced but should be excluded from primary evidence — they are not authoritative sources for case counts.
- The DSHS Strategic Plan PDF and TSHAC meeting minutes (also surfaced) are not relevant to measles case data and should be excluded from the candidate set during downstream processing.
decision.disease_location_time_fit_assessment:
Excellent fit across all three dimensions:
- **Disease**: All accepted candidates are explicitly about measles (rubeola) — no off-topic disease contamination.
- **Location**: Texas is the primary location in all key candidates. Subnational locations (Gaines County, South Plains, Lubbock, Harris County, Seminole) are well-documented. The multi-state outbreak context (New Mexico, Oklahoma) is present in some sources but Texas-specific figures are clearly distinguished.
- **Time window (Jan 1–Apr 30 2025)**: All key data points fall within the task window. The DSHS main outbreak page was last updated Aug 12 2025 (post-window), but its referenced press releases (Feb 26, Apr 6) and the MMWR reports (covering through Apr 17) are within the window. Care will be needed during data extraction to restrict to Jan 1–Apr 30 2025 data points only — particularly for the DSHS main page which covers the full outbreak arc through August.
decision.corroboration_potential_assessment:
High corroboration achieved across independent source types:
- **Primary official (DSHS)**: Main outbreak page, second-death press release, Harris County January alert, SPPHD PDF, News & Alerts index — all from dshs.texas.gov.
- **Federal official (CDC MMWR)**: Three distinct MMWR reports covering different sub-periods (mm7520a1: Jan 20–Mar 18; mm7523a2: Jan 29–Feb 28; mm7414a1: Jan 1–Apr 17) provide cross-validated case and death counts.
- **Hospital/clinical**: Texas Children's Hospital page (Apr 15 snapshot, 561 cases) corroborates DSHS figures.
- **News/media**: Texas Tribune (2 results), NBC News tracker, CIDRAP (2 results), ABC News — all citing official figures, providing dated evidence quotes and locality detail.
- **Academic/public health**: PMC article, TEPHI, JHU Public Health — secondary corroboration.
- **International**: WHO and PAHO results from iter1 provide international validation layer.

The three independent authoritative count series (DSHS press releases, CDC MMWR sub-period reports, CDC national tracker) are mutually consistent and cover the full Jan–Apr 2025 window without contradictions in the available snippets.
